title: How to Appraise Your Organization's Capabilities and Disabilities
hook: What made you good at this work is not the same as what will make you good at that work.
counterintuition: The self-appraisal problem is not whether the organization has strong capabilities. The problem is that those capabilities were built to produce a specific kind of result in a specific context. When the context changes, the capability continues producing what it was designed to produce, which in fact may no longer be the right thing.
tryThisNow: Name one organizational routine your team does exceptionally well. Write down the underlying assumption that routine makes about what a good outcome looks like. Then write one sentence about whether a new market you are considering shares that assumption.
keyTakeaway: Capabilities embed assumptions about what good work looks like. Fit appraisal asks whether the new context shares those assumptions. Strength in one setting can be an obstacle in another.

breakdown.fastRead:
Organizational capabilities are built to produce specific kinds of results in specific kinds of contexts. A pharmaceutical company's drug development process is excellent at producing safe, rigorously validated products because it was built to meet the standards that market requires. A legal firm's billable-hour discipline is excellent at ensuring that research quality is tracked and compensated because the billing model rewards it. These are real strengths. They are also routines: systematic ways of doing work that embed assumptions about what good outcomes look like.

When an organization enters a new context, those routines move with it. What does not automatically move is the match between what the routine produces and what the new context needs. A pharmaceutical process designed for eighteen-month iteration cycles arrives in a consumer wellness market where competitors iterate in three months. The process is just as good as it was. The context has different requirements.

A capability is context-dependent. What it enables in one setting, it may block in another.
breakdown.deepRead:
The self-appraisal problem is not a question of whether the organization has capable people or well-designed processes. Most organizations that are excellent at what they currently do have both. The problem is that capability is always relative to a task and a context. A capability that fits the current task precisely may not fit a new task at all, not because the capability degraded, but because it was built for a different set of requirements.

Routines are the most visible form of this. An organization's routines embed decisions about what matters: how quickly outputs need to be produced, what quality standards apply, what a successful outcome looks like to the customer who will use it. Those decisions were made, consciously or not, in response to the requirements of the current market. The routine optimizes for what the current market rewards. It is not designed to re-evaluate that optimization when the market changes.

The routine has not failed. The context has changed.

What makes this difficult is that the same routine that is an obstacle in the new context is a strength in the existing one. Removing it to enter the new context would degrade performance in the place where it is working. Keeping it blocks entry into the place where it is not. The appraisal question is not 'is this capability good?' The appraisal question is: does this capability fit what the new task specifically requires?
breakdown.fullRead:
Think of one thing your organization does exceptionally well. Not a general attribute: a specific routine or process. How long does it take to validate a new product claim? How many approvals does a customer communication go through before it ships? What is the standard for how a recommendation gets written and presented? These routines produce outcomes your organization values, which is why they exist. They were built to produce those outcomes reliably.

Now think about what assumption that routine makes about what a good outcome looks like. The validation timeline assumes that accuracy is worth the time it takes. The approval process assumes that the risk of miscommunication exceeds the cost of delay. The recommendation standard assumes that the work will be handed off rather than owned. These assumptions are embedded so deeply that the routine does not surface them as assumptions. They are simply how things get done. Ask why the validation takes as long as it does, and the answer is: because that is the standard. The standard does not explain itself. It was formed in a context that no longer needs explaining.

When that routine moves into a new context, the assumption moves with it. A new context may have a different view of what accuracy is worth, what delay costs, or who owns the output. If it does, the routine will produce exactly what it was designed to produce, and the new context will treat that output as a performance problem rather than a quality signal. The routine is not broken. It is producing what it was built to produce. The problem is that the new context has different requirements.

Kathryn's automation platform arrived in a firm whose billable-hour culture treated research efficiency as a problem rather than an asset. The platform was good. The firm's discipline was real. The assumption that high-quality work requires time investment was embedded in every associate's understanding of what they were being paid to produce. The platform could not change that assumption. The capability mismatch was not visible in any performance metric. It was visible in the utilization log.

The question is not whether the organization is capable. It is whether the capability fits the task.

Fit appraisal requires naming the assumption before assessing the capability. What does this routine optimize for? What does the new task require? If those two answers are the same, the capability is likely to transfer. If they are different, the capability that looks like a strength in the existing context is likely to produce the obstacle in the new one. That is not a critique of the capability. It is an observation about where it was built to work.

examples.title: Kathryn's Platform Dashboard Shows 22 Percent Utilization

planSpec.domain: law firm entering legal research automation and discovering that billable-hour culture conflicts with the automation model
planSpec.audience: a managing partner leading the firm's investment in a legal research automation platform
planSpec.stakes: the platform reduces research time, which reduces billable hours under the current billing model
planSpec.requiredBeat: Kathryn discovers that associates are not using the automation platform to its potential because the billable-hour structure rewards time-intensive research over efficient research.
mustInclude: the quality-discipline framing of the original strength
mustAvoid: implying billable-hour billing is inherently corrupt or outdated

examples.scenario: "Why are the associates still spending three hours on cases the platform should answer in thirty minutes?" the senior partner asks. Kathryn looks at the platform utilization dashboard: 22 percent active use across the associate pool. The platform is working. The research it generates is accurate. The associates are accurate too, and they are producing more billable hours by doing research the slow way. The billing model rewards thorough, time-documented work. The platform's efficiency benefit is a reduction in the metric the culture is built to protect.
examples.whatToDo: Identify whether the billing model needs to change before the platform can produce its intended benefit. The utilization problem is not a technology problem. The billing structure rewards the behavior the platform is designed to replace.
examples.whyItMatters: A platform that reduces research time reduces billable hours under the current billing model. The culture built around billable-hour excellence is the obstacle to the efficiency the platform offers. Both are real. They are incompatible.

examples.title: Thomas's Supplement Line Arrives After Competitors Have Set the Price Point

planSpec.domain: pharmaceutical company entering consumer wellness supplements and discovering that drug-development discipline mismatches consumer speed
planSpec.audience: a VP of business development whose division has approved a consumer wellness line using the drug development governance process
planSpec.stakes: the drug-development approval timeline is twelve to eighteen months per product; consumer wellness competitors iterate in three months
planSpec.requiredBeat: Thomas's team produces a supplement line that has been through more safety and quality review than any competitor's product. By the time it reaches market, competitors have already iterated twice and own the customer relationships.
mustInclude: safety and quality review as the strength
competitor relationship ownership as the consequence
mustAvoid: suggesting that pharmaceutical safety review should be shortened

examples.scenario: Looking back at the wellness supplement launch timeline, Thomas can trace every delay to a process doing its job correctly. The safety review was thorough. The regulatory documentation was complete. The quality testing met pharmaceutical standards. Consumer wellness competitors who arrived nine months earlier had a shorter version of each review and were iterating on customer feedback while Thomas's team completed its third compliance cycle. The product reached market with better documentation than any competitor's and arrived after they had already set the price point.
examples.whatToDo: Map the pharmaceutical process timeline against competitor iteration speed before applying it to the next product. The process fits pharmaceutical standards. It may not fit the consumer market's competitive tempo.
examples.whyItMatters: A development process built for pharmaceutical precision produces pharmaceutical timing. Consumer wellness competitors iterate faster. The process produces excellent quality and creates a competitive timing obstacle. Both are true.

examples.title: Hugo's Charging Network App Prototype Meets the Dealer Agreement Clause

planSpec.domain: automotive OEM entering EV charging network infrastructure and discovering that dealer relationship governance conflicts with direct-to-driver service
planSpec.audience: a VP of digital services whose EV charging network requires direct consumer app relationships that the dealer agreement structure prohibits
planSpec.stakes: the OEM's dealer network is one of its core competitive assets; the EV charging model requires a consumer relationship the dealer agreement prevents
planSpec.requiredBeat: Hugo sees that the charging network requires a direct consumer relationship that the dealer agreement prohibits. The decision forces a confrontation with which capability is load-bearing and which is context-dependent.
mustInclude: consumer data clause as the obstacle
mustAvoid: portraying dealers as obstructionist rather than contractually protected

examples.scenario: At 9:00 a.m., Hugo opens the EV charging network app prototype alongside the dealer agreement's clause on consumer data ownership. The prototype requires direct consumer registration, usage history, and payment processing. The dealer agreement assigns consumer data rights to dealer franchisees, not to the OEM. Hugo's team has spent four months building a direct driver relationship into an application that the dealer network agreement prohibits. The decision is now structural, not technical.
examples.whatToDo: Identify whether a structural arrangement exists that captures the direct consumer relationship requirement without violating the dealer agreement's terms before building further into the current structure.
examples.whyItMatters: A dealer network is a real competitive asset and a set of agreements that define how the OEM can relate to consumers. In a market requiring direct consumer data, those agreements prohibit the capability the new service requires.

examples.title: Petra's Newsletter Is the Most Rigorously Sourced and the Slowest

planSpec.domain: broadcast journalist entering newsletter journalism and discovering that broadcast sourcing and editorial rhythms misfit newsletter cadence
planSpec.audience: a senior broadcast journalist with thirty years of source relationships and editorial process discipline
planSpec.stakes: newsletter readers expect daily updates; broadcast editorial discipline requires multi-source verification that produces newsletter content too slowly
planSpec.requiredBeat: Petra predicts her source network and editorial standards will be competitive advantages in newsletter journalism. The reveal: her newsletter arrives two days after competitors have already set the conversation.
mustInclude: competitor conversation ownership in the reveal
mustAvoid: suggesting that multi-source verification is journalistically wrong

examples.scenario: What does a broadcast journalist with thirty years of source relationships and a multi-source verification standard bring to newsletter journalism? Petra's newsletter has the most rigorously sourced content in its category. It also publishes two days after competitors have already set the story. Her verification standard requires three independent source confirmations. By the time she has the third, the story has moved. Petra predicted her sourcing network would be a competitive advantage. Subscriber growth is going to the faster writers.
examples.whatToDo: Define what accuracy standard the newsletter's readers require before applying the broadcast verification cadence. The broadcast and newsletter formats have different speed-accuracy trade-offs. The standard should fit the format.
examples.whyItMatters: A verification standard built for broadcast journalism produces broadcast-quality content on a broadcast timeline. In a format where recency matters, that timeline is a competitive disadvantage. The strength is real. The fit is not.

examples.title: Diego's All-Hands Deck Is Forty Slides and Nobody Owns Slide 28

planSpec.domain: management consultant joining an early-stage company as COO and discovering that consulting deliverable culture mismatches operational ownership
planSpec.audience: a former partner at a consulting firm taking the COO role at a 30-person software company
planSpec.stakes: consulting excellence requires polished recommendations built for handoff; COO work requires owning and implementing what you recommend
planSpec.requiredBeat: Diego's postmortem shows his analysis quality was high and his recommendation precision was excellent. It also shows that every recommendation was written for handoff rather than ownership.
mustInclude: analysis and recommendation quality as genuine strength
the consulting-exit posture in the deliverable
mustAvoid: suggesting that consulting skills are generally inferior to operational skills

examples.scenario: The all-hands deck is forty slides, each section argued with data and a recommendation on the last page. Diego has delivered presentations like this for eleven years. The software company's team is asking who implements slide 28. His postmortem on the first six months shows excellent analysis quality and precise recommendations. Every recommendation was written for handoff rather than ownership: framed for an executive who would assign the work, not for the person doing it the next morning.
examples.whatToDo: Rebuild the next recommendation as an implementation plan with named owners before presenting it. The analytical quality is not the problem. The deliverable structure is optimized for handoff, not for the person who owns the execution.
examples.whyItMatters: A consulting deliverable is built for handoff. An operational plan is built for ownership. The same analytical quality produces a different kind of document depending on which context it is written for.

examples.title: Layla's Custom Details Are the Factory's Variance Problem

planSpec.domain: licensed architect entering prefab modular housing design and discovering that custom-design discipline mismatches manufacturing tolerance requirements
planSpec.audience: a principal architect whose studio has a reputation for bespoke residential design
planSpec.stakes: modular manufacturing requires standardized component tolerances; bespoke design expertise produces custom-optimized solutions that manufacturing cannot reproduce consistently at scale
planSpec.requiredBeat: Before: Layla designs the modular housing unit with the same site-specific optimization that has won her studio commissions. After: the manufacturing partner shows which design decisions cannot be repeated at required tolerance.
mustInclude: bespoke design as the studio's competitive strength
the explicit before/after of what the detail means in each context
mustAvoid: suggesting that bespoke architecture is inherently better or worse than modular design

examples.scenario: You are walking through Layla's studio portfolio: twelve residential commissions with site-specific solutions that no two look the same. Before: Layla applies the same custom-optimization discipline to the modular housing design. Each unit has a site-specific structural decision and a custom facade detail. After: the manufacturing partner's review marks fifteen variance flags across the first design package. Every custom decision is a production deviation. The studio's competitive strength is the factory's most significant production problem.
examples.whatToDo: Identify which design decisions can be standardized before the next design package. The studio's discipline produces excellent bespoke work. Manufacturing requires repeatable precision, which is a different definition of quality.
examples.whyItMatters: Bespoke design and manufacturing have different definitions of quality. A studio that optimized for differentiation will generate the factory's variance problems. Both sides are correct within their own definition.

questions.prompt: What makes an organizational capability context-dependent rather than universally applicable?
choices: Capabilities are context-dependent only because organizations are too large to change quickly, and this limitation disappears when organizations build internal agility mechanisms or reduce bureaucratic layers.

A capability was built to produce a specific kind of result in a specific context. It embeds assumptions about what a good outcome looks like. When the context changes, those assumptions may not match the new requirements.
Context-dependence applies only to process capabilities, not to individual people capabilities, since individuals can adapt to new environments through training and professional development.
questions.explanation: Organizational capabilities are not abstract strengths. They are routines and processes built to produce specific results in specific conditions. The conditions those capabilities were built for may not apply in a new context, even if the capabilities themselves remain strong.

questions.prompt: A pharmaceutical company applies its drug development governance process to a consumer wellness supplement line. The product reaches market 18 months after competitors who iterated in 3 months. What specific capability mismatch explains the outcome?
choices: The pharmaceutical division lacked sufficient motivation and competitive awareness to adjust its development timeline for the consumer wellness market, despite having the underlying technical capabilities.

The consumer wellness market requires drug-level validation standards, which the company correctly applied because consumer health products and pharmaceuticals share the same fundamental safety obligations.

The drug development process embeds an assumption that iteration speed is worth sacrificing for thoroughness. The consumer wellness market rewards iteration speed above the thoroughness level the pharmaceutical process provides.
questions.explanation: The pharmaceutical process is not wrong for the pharmaceutical market. It embeds an assumption about what quality requires. The consumer wellness market embeds a different assumption. The process transferred. The assumption mismatch did not resolve.

questions.prompt: A senior broadcast journalist applies her multi-source verification standard to a newsletter. Her newsletter consistently arrives two days after competitors have set the conversation. What does this reveal about her verification standard?
choices: The verification standard was built for broadcast accuracy requirements. Newsletter readers reward recency at a different speed threshold. The same standard that produces authoritative broadcast journalism produces slow newsletter content.
Her verification standard is too rigorous for any journalism context and should be reduced across all reporting formats to enable faster publication and audience engagement.
The outcome reveals that she has insufficient sources for the newsletter journalism format specifically, and she should develop a dedicated source network suited to faster publication cycles.
questions.explanation: Multi-source verification is not wrong as a journalism standard. It embeds an assumption about what accuracy requires and what delay is acceptable. The newsletter context has a different speed-accuracy trade-off than broadcast journalism. The standard transferred. The fit did not.

questions.prompt: A consulting partner takes a COO role at a 30-person software company. Six months in, her recommendations are analytically excellent but consistently written as if someone else will implement them. What capability mismatch does this reflect?
choices: She lacks the analytical depth and operational experience needed to run a software company, and the COO role requires a fundamentally different orientation toward ownership and execution than consulting has developed in her.

Consulting excellence requires polished deliverables built for handoff. COO work requires owning and revising the output in real time. The same deliverable quality that distinguishes a consulting engagement signals the wrong relationship to ownership in an operational role.

The company's team is not capable of executing the recommendations she provides, and the organization needs to hire additional operational staff who can implement complex strategic initiatives without requiring detailed handoff documentation.
questions.explanation: The consultant's analytical and communication capabilities are genuine strengths. They were built for a context where the deliverable is handed to a client who implements it. In an operational role, the output must be built to be owned and revised. The capability exists. The assumption about who owns the output does not fit.

questions.prompt: A law firm implements a legal research automation platform. Platform utilization is 22 percent six months after deployment. Associates are not using the efficiency gain. What capability mismatch is most likely driving the low utilization?
choices: The platform is too technically complex and poorly documented for associates to adopt without additional training and sustained technical support from the implementation team.

The firm's partners have not communicated the business case for using the platform clearly or consistently enough, and associates would adopt it more readily with better internal messaging about its purpose.

The firm's billable-hour culture treats time-efficient research as a reduction in billable output. The capability that makes associates excellent researchers (disciplined, time-documented work) is the obstacle to the platform's intended benefit.
questions.explanation: The automation platform reduces research time, which under billable-hour accounting reduces billable output. The culture treats thoroughness and time investment as signs of quality. The platform's efficiency benefit is at odds with the assumption the billing model rewards. The culture is operating exactly as designed. The design does not fit the new tool.

questions.prompt: Why can the same organizational routine be a genuine strength in one context and a genuine obstacle in another?
choices: Because routines embed assumptions about what a good outcome looks like that were formed in the current context. A new context may have different requirements, and the routine will continue producing what it was designed to produce regardless.

Because organizational routines are inherently conservative and resist any market change, since they are designed to preserve the performance standards that proved effective in the conditions where they were originally built.

Because context-dependent capabilities only appear in industries with high regulatory requirements, where external compliance mandates make it difficult to modify established processes in response to market shifts.
questions.explanation: Routines do not evaluate whether they are appropriate to a new context. They produce what they were designed to produce. If the new context has different requirements, the routine continues to satisfy the old context's requirements. That is not inertia. It is the routine performing correctly in the conditions for which it was built.

questions.prompt: An automotive OEM's dealer network is one of its strongest competitive assets. The OEM is entering an EV charging network that requires direct consumer app relationships. The dealer agreement prohibits direct consumer data access. What does this situation reveal about the dealer network capability?
choices: The dealer network should be dissolved or substantially restructured so the OEM can build the direct consumer relationships that the EV charging market requires.

The dealer network is a genuine competitive asset in automotive distribution. In the EV charging context, the same network's legal structure is the obstacle to the capability the new service requires. The asset is context-dependent.

The dealer network's value was always overstated and the EV market entry is revealing that its competitive advantages were largely a product of regulatory protection rather than inherent market strength.
questions.explanation: A dealer network is a real competitive asset in automotive distribution. It is also a set of agreements that define how the OEM can and cannot relate to consumers. In a context that requires direct consumer relationships, those agreements are the obstacle. The asset did not become worthless. Its context changed.

questions.prompt: An architect enters prefab modular housing design. Her bespoke design discipline has generated her studio's reputation. The manufacturing partner marks up her designs with variance flags: every custom detail is a production deviation. What is the root explanation?
choices: The architect lacks the technical knowledge needed to design for manufacturing tolerances and should partner with a structural engineer who specializes in prefab systems before producing further design packages.

Prefab modular manufacturing is fundamentally incompatible with high-quality architecture, because the standardization required for factory production eliminates the design decisions that give buildings their identity.

Her studio's competitive strength, custom-optimization for each site and client, embeds an assumption that quality means differentiation. Manufacturing quality means repeatable precision. The two assumptions conflict at every custom detail.
questions.explanation: The architect's bespoke design capability is a genuine professional strength. It embeds an assumption that quality equals differentiation. Manufacturing tolerances require the opposite assumption: quality equals repeatability. Both are correct definitions of quality within their respective contexts. The capability mismatch is between two different, context-specific definitions of excellent work.

questions.prompt: A CEO argues that a strong organizational capability is valuable regardless of context because capability is a relative advantage over less capable competitors. How should this argument be assessed?
choices: The argument correctly identifies relative advantage but misses the specificity of fit. A capability can be stronger than a competitor's and still misfit the requirements of a new task. Relative strength does not substitute for fit with what the task requires.

The argument is correct: relative capability advantage is always more important than task-specific fit, because superior capabilities will outperform context-specific alternatives over any sustained competitive period.

The argument is wrong: capability has no meaningful value unless it is a sufficiently close match for the task requirements, and organizations should only enter markets where their existing capabilities already apply.
questions.explanation: Relative advantage matters in competitive markets. Fit appraisal addresses a different question: whether the task can be done well with the capabilities the organization has, regardless of what competitors have. A firm can be the strongest player in the room and still fail the task if its capabilities were built for a different one.

reviewCards.front: What does it mean for an organizational capability to be context-dependent?
reviewCards.back: A context-dependent capability was built to produce results in a specific setting. It embeds assumptions about what quality, speed, and a good outcome look like. When the setting changes, the capability continues producing what it was designed for, which may not be what the new context requires.

reviewCards.front: A routine in your organization produces excellent results in the current market. You are entering a new one. What question should you ask about the routine first?
reviewCards.back: What assumption does this routine make about what a good outcome looks like? And does the new market share that assumption? If it does not, the routine will produce what it was designed to produce, not what the new market needs.

reviewCards.front: Why is it insufficient to ask 'is this organization capable?' when appraising fit for a new market?
reviewCards.back: Capability is always relative to a task. A capable organization may have processes and routines that fit the current task precisely and mismatch the new one exactly. The useful question is whether its specific capabilities fit what the new task requires.

reviewCards.front: A team's core strength becomes an obstacle when entering a new market. Does this mean the strength should be abandoned?
reviewCards.back: No. The strength may be load-bearing in the current market. The appraisal question is whether the new task can be structured to work around the mismatch, not whether to discard a genuine asset. Context-dependence is an observation about fit, not a verdict on value.

reviewCards.front: An organization is appraising whether its capabilities fit a new market. It asks 'are we capable?' instead of the right question. What should it ask instead?
reviewCards.back: Fit appraisal matches specific organizational capabilities against the specific requirements of a new task. It answers: does this organization's current set of routines, processes, and values fit what this new context requires, or does a specific mismatch need to be named and addressed?

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to identify the assumptions embedded in your organization's best routines and appraise whether those assumptions match what a new market or task requires.

ifThenPlans.context: entering a new market with an existing organizational capability
ifThenPlans.plan: If a capability is being applied to a new market, then name the assumption the capability embeds about what a good outcome looks like and assess whether the new market shares that assumption before committing to the capability transfer.

ifThenPlans.context: a strong organizational process is producing poor results in a new context
ifThenPlans.plan: If a well-established process is not performing as expected in a new context, then investigate whether the process is producing exactly what it was designed to produce but the new context requires something different, before treating the issue as a process failure.

ifThenPlans.context: evaluating whether to bring a high-capability specialist from a different industry
ifThenPlans.plan: If a specialist brings strong capabilities from a different industry context, then assess which of their capabilities were built for that industry's specific requirements and whether those requirements apply in the new context.

ifThenPlans.context: assessing organizational readiness to enter a new market
ifThenPlans.plan: If the team is appraising readiness for a new market, then list the two or three most important routines that drive current performance and explicitly state the assumption each routine makes about what a good outcome looks like. Then test whether the new market shares those assumptions.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Name one organizational routine your team does exceptionally well. Write down the underlying assumption that routine makes about what a good outcome looks like. Then write one sentence about whether a new market you are considering shares that assumption.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, when a new initiative is being assessed, identify the two most important organizational routines that would be applied and ask whether those routines were built for the current context's requirements or the new one's.

memorableLines.text: A capability is context-dependent. What it enables in one setting, it may block in another.
memorableLines.why: Converts the chapter's core mechanism into a two-sentence rule that applies directly to any capability appraisal.

memorableLines.text: The routine has not failed. The context has changed.
memorableLines.why: Reframes what looks like a performance failure as a context mismatch without excusing poor results.

memorableLines.text: The question is not whether the organization is capable. It is whether the capability fits the task.
memorableLines.why: Converts the appraisal problem from a general-strength question to a specific-fit question.
